name: Windsor Tan
lede: Windsor Tan is a deep orange-brown that Maerz and Paul recorded in 1925, sharing the "Windsor" family name with an unrelated dark purple of the same catalogue rather than with any tan.

sections.title: A 1925 entry in the Windsor family
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary records Windsor Tan as first listed in 1925, and the ISCC-NBS system later filed it as a deep orange [1]. Our records for this entry do not preserve a plate position, unlike several of its Windsor-family neighbors [1]. As with [[windsor-green|Windsor Green]], the shared "Windsor" word is a family label across several catalogue names, not a description of hue: the base color Windsor itself, also from Maerz and Paul, is a dark grayish purple [2].

Its closest named relatives by measured color are [[windsor-tan]] and [[brown-orange]], both within about 4 units [3].

Further out are [[burnt-sienna]], more vivid at 4.4 units, and [[orange-brown]], duller at 5.6 [3]. Our library files the color under fashion and textiles[1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, a color within six units of Windsor Tan covers at least five per cent of a canvas in 188 works, peaking in the 1820s at over six times the archive's overall rate [4]. George Dawe is the strongest match, present in six of his fifty archived paintings, over fifteen times the expected rate, and a 1680 Ragamala page carries it across nearly 60 per cent of the canvas [4]. It most often shares a canvas with marigold and sienna [4]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment tests [4]. Across its matches, coverage splits almost evenly between mid-tone and highlight, with very little in shadow [4]. By century, the color is present even in the 1200s, well before Maerz and Paul's own 1925 record date, at over two and a half times the archive's overall rate for that period [4].
